results.text: Calendly sells per-seat subscriptions across four tiers: a free plan, Standard at $10 per seat per month, Teams at $16, and Enterprise starting at $15k a year.
The prices shown by default are annual rates; paying monthly costs $12 and $20 per seat.
The new AI products are sold as a packaging upgrade rather than a separate add-on: turning on Notetaker and Callie switches the plans to Standard Plus at $18 and Teams Plus at $24 per seat per month.

The AI packaging raises the list price of a paid seat by 80% on Standard ($10 to $18) and 50% on Teams ($16 to $24), which makes existing paid users, not new signups, the most likely source of near-term revenue growth.
Headline per-seat list prices have not moved in nearly two years, so the Plus tiers are where the price increase went.
The motion is hybrid: self-serve through Teams, sales-led at Enterprise, with the handover pinned to a 50-seat floor.
Pricing is published in three currencies as separate list prices rather than as a converted figure.
Whether Calendly takes a cut of the payments its customers collect is unknown.
Calendly now claims the category of AI meeting management alongside scheduling, with the homepage promising that the whole job around a meeting is handled.
The repositioning happened between 1 July and 1 October 2026 and replaced a pitch that had been stable for at least eighteen months.
The homepage still leads on scheduling leadership, which reads as using the existing market position as the entry point to the AI story rather than replacing it.
Social proof on the public site shifted from organisation counts to raw scale, with the Fortune 500 claim moved off the homepage onto the enterprise page.
The relaunch has not reached the rest of the site: the enterprise page, the comparison hub and the founder's own bio still carry the old pitch and old numbers.
Calendly's four biggest organic rivals are not the tools its comparison hub positions against.
The public customer proof is mostly solo operators and very small businesses, which sits oddly against an enterprise tier that starts at 50 seats.
Organic search is the largest acquisition channel this capture can measure.
Most of that search demand is people looking for Calendly by name, so it is a measure of brand strength more than of content discovery.
Most of Calendly's non-branded search traffic comes from short generic head terms it holds at position 1, not from long-tail content.
The blog is a quarter of the site's pages but earns only a sliver of its search traffic, so the content library is not carrying acquisition.
Customers' own Calendly booking pages rank in Google and pull in a measurable share of the domain's search traffic.
LinkedIn is the only platform where Calendly's own ads were found, and the creative splits three ways: team-oriented product ads, a thought-leadership video series and recruitment ads.

results.text: Neither Meta's nor Google's ad library shows ads from a Calendly-named advertiser, so no live spend on either platform is visible — and no Meta pixel was detected on the site at all.
Paid advertising appears to be a minor channel for Calendly relative to its scale, though pauses, regional targeting and unverified advertiser accounts could all hide spend the libraries do not show.
Thousands of other advertisers' ads point at calendly.com, most likely because customers use their booking links as ad landing pages — a distribution loop the company gets for free.
A visitor-identification tool and a review-site intent tag are installed across the site, which is the setup for routing interested companies to sales.
Behind the consumer-looking homepage sits a conventional B2B demand-gen library aimed at departments and industries.
No marketing, sales or support roles are open: the 8 open roles are all engineering, product and security, and three of them name AI work directly.
How much Calendly spends on acquisition, and on which campaigns, is unknown.
The primary conversion is a free account created with a Google or Microsoft login, which doubles as the calendar connection the product needs.
The signup page leads with a free account but merchandises a 14-day Teams Plus trial alongside it, using the AI features and branding removal as the premium hook.
The sales form is short: five fields, one qualifying question, and seat band is the only qualification asked for.
Leads are captured into Marketo and the field names indicate a Salesforce back end.
An A/B testing tool runs on every captured page, so what any given visitor sees may differ from this capture.
Conversion research and live chat run alongside the tests on the marketing site.
Tracking is routed through Calendly's own subdomains, which keeps analytics and ad measurement working against ad blockers and browser cookie limits.
Which conversion events Calendly optimises toward could not be observed.
The product-data stack is mature and built for lifecycle work: a CDP feeding product analytics, with marketing automation alongside.
Self-serve support is the single largest content investment on the site, which is what a product with tens of millions of low-touch users requires.

results.text: A 19-page learning hub sits on the main site and a separate community subdomain earns its own search traffic.
Recent customer stories lead with the new AI products, which looks like merchandising adoption to the existing base.
Churn, retention and expansion rates are unknown.
Calendly publishes rarely now — about 13 posts across the eight months to October 2026.

results.text: Recent posts are product marketing, not search bait: almost everything published in 2026 explains a new Calendly capability or integration.
An AI-integration cluster has emerged as the one genuinely new content bet, positioning Calendly as the scheduling layer other AI tools call.
The blog pages that earn search traffic are generic calendar and productivity guides unrelated to the new AI positioning.
Posts hand readers to a free signup rather than to a gated asset; no lead-capture form appeared in any sampled post.
The bottom-of-funnel comparison cluster has been left to go stale even though it still ranks.
Authorship spans marketing and engineering, which suggests the blog is now used as a company channel rather than an SEO channel.
For most of the archived period Calendly sold one thing — easy scheduling — and the pitch barely moved.
In the quarter to 1 October 2026 the company rewrote the homepage end to end, tripling its length and swapping the category from scheduling software to AI meeting tools.
The pricing page was rewritten in the same quarter, turning from a plan chooser into an upsell page for the new AI products.
Through all of it the price card stayed put, so Calendly chose to monetise the AI launch through new Plus tiers instead of raising the price of what people already bought.
Maze entered the homepage HTML during 2025 as Optimizely dropped out of it, which points to a change in the experimentation and research stack.
Ketch and Marketo appear in the homepage HTML for the first time in the October 2026 copy, alongside the new positioning.
